Research in Brief
Strategies to develop therapeutic cancer vaccines for pancreatic cancer
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies. Conventional immunotherapies have shown little clinical benefit, largely due to the low neoantigenicity and profoundly immunosuppressive microenvironment of this cancer. Therapeutic cancer vaccines have emerged as a rational strategy to prime or amplify antitumour immunity, supported by advances in antigen discovery, genomic profiling, and vaccine engineering. Here, we report a review of clinical trials evaluating therapeutic cancer vaccines in PDAC. Eligible studies were identified through searches of ClinicalTrials.gov from database inception to Aug 31, 2025, with manual screening of trial-linked publications up to Jan 31, 2026. 135 records were identified, of which 120 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Across vaccine platforms-cell-based, nucleic acid-based, protein and peptide-based, microorganism-based, and multiplatform strategies-early-phase clinical studies consistently show feasibility, favourable safety profiles, and the induction of tumour-specific immune responses. However, immune activation has rarely translated into durable clinical benefit. To date, the most compelling biological signals derive from personalised neoantigen vaccines, particularly mRNA-based approaches, which can elicit high-magnitude CD8 + T-cell responses and long-lived clonal persistence in postoperative PDAC. Emerging evidence also supports the potential of shared neoantigens, such as KRAS mut , as biologically relevant and scalable targets. Collectively, our findings highlight a shift towards rational vaccine combination strategies aimed at overcoming stromal and myeloid-mediated immunosuppression. Future progress will depend on integrating therapeutic vaccination into multimodal regimens and evaluating these approaches in adequately powered, biomarker-selected clinical trials.

title: Thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist simedeutirom (HSK31679) for Chinese patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis: a 52-week, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial
abstract: Background Simedeutirom is a selective thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist that has previously been shown to reduce hepatic fat content in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. We assessed the efficacy and safety of simedeutirom in patients of Asian descent with biopsy-confirmed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and F2 or F3 fibrosis. Methods This multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial was conducted at 42 clinical sites in China. Adults (aged 18-74 years) with biopsy-confirmed MASH, a non-alcoholic fatty liver disease activity score (NAS) of at least 4, F2 or F3 fibrosis, and MRI-proton density fat fraction liver fat content of at least 8% were randomly assigned (1:1:1) by block randomisation (block size of six; no stratification) via a centralised web-based system to receive once-daily simedeutirom 80 mg, simedeutirom 160 mg, or placebo for 52 weeks. Participants and study personnel were masked to treatment assignment. The primary endpoint was MASH improvement (ie, two-point or more reduction in NAS, one-point or more improvement in hepatocellular ballooning, and no increase in steatosis score) without worsening of fibrosis (ie, no increase in fibrosis stage) at week 52. Efficacy was analysed in the full analysis set, which included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose and had at least one efficacy assessment after baseline; participants without liver biopsy data after treatment or who used prohibited medications affecting efficacy were considered non-responders. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06168383) and is complete. Findings Between Jan 5, 2024, and Jan 16, 2026, 186 participants were randomly assigned (62 per group). In the full analysis set (n=179), the median age was 42·0 years (IQR 35·0-54·0), 116 (65%) participants were men, and 63 (35%) were women. 22 (37%) of 59 participants in the 80 mg group, 18 (30%) of 60 in the 160 mg group, and six (10%) of 60 in the placebo group had MASH improvement without worsening of fibrosis at week 52. ORs versus placebo were 4·87 (95% CI 1·76-13·48; p=0·0023) in the 80 mg group and 5·24 (1·74-15·72; p=0·0032) in the 160 mg group, with absolute differences of 27·3 percentage points (95% CI 12·2-41·1) and 20·0 percentage points (5·7-33·6), respectively. Grade 3 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in three (5%) of 61 participants in the simedeutirom 80 mg group, five (8%) of 62 in the simedeutirom 160 mg group, and three (5%) of 62 in the placebo group; no individual grade 3 event affected more than one participant, and no grade 4-5 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred. Serious adverse events occurred in three (5%) participants in the simedeutirom 80 mg group, four (6%) in the simedeutirom 160 mg group, and three (5%) in the placebo group; none were treatment related. No deaths or adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation occurred. Interpretation Simedeutirom led to higher rates of MASH improvement without worsening of fibrosis than placebo after 52 weeks, warranting further investigation in phase 3 trials. Funding Haisco Pharmaceutical Group.

title: THR-β agonism in MASH: expanding the evidence to Asia
Updated treatment targets in inflammatory bowel disease (STRIDE-III): an initiative of the International Organization for the Study of IBD
abstract: Since Selecting Therapeutic Targets in Inflammatory Bowel Disease-II (STRIDE-II), new evidence has become available across inflammatory and patient-centred outcomes. We aimed to update the STRIDE recommendations for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL for studies published after the STRIDE-II search period. Findings were integrated with surveys of International Organization for the Study of IBD (IOIBD) members and paediatric gastroenterologists from the Porto group of the European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition. Statements were subsequently voted on using a modified Delphi approach; consensus was defined as ≥75% of participants rating a statement 7-10 on a 10-point scale. Of 13 071 records identified in the systematic review, 1018 were included. Surveys were completed by 60 of 79 IOIBD gastroenterologists and 23 of 30 paediatric gastroenterologists in the Porto group. STRIDE-III defines three conceptually distinct categories of treatment targets. Actionable targets include clinical response and remission, which reflect patient priorities, and objective inflammatory targets (C-reactive protein normalisation, faecal calprotectin within target range, and endoscopic remission), supported by interventional evidence demonstrating benefits of target-guided treatment modification. Adjunctive targets (ie, urgency, histological remission in ulcerative colitis, transmural remission in Crohn's disease, and growth) are supported by studies showing association with favourable outcomes and guide treatment optimisation and tighter monitoring but do not necessarily require a change in therapeutic class. Patient-centred targets (ie, disability, fatigue, and quality of life) directly reflect patients' well-being and are impaired in a substantial proportion of patients with inflammatory bowel disease; impairment should prompt assessment of inflammation and alternative causes and management through shared decision-making. Targets are further classified as immediate, short-term, intermediate, and long-term. STRIDE-III also defines treatment-specific times to target achievement, new faecal calprotectin thresholds, and adaptations for resource-limited settings. STRIDE-III distinguishes targets that should prompt treatment change from those that primarily guide optimisation and monitoring, while establishing a separate patient-centred pathway based on shared decision-making. This framework supports consistent, evidence-based treat-to-target care.
